rows.en: From all these considerations we can hold it as clear that from the very first, that is, from the time when the statutes and teachings of God were written in a book, various traditions were known by which a number of statutes in the Torah were understood; and we will say even more: that they were the pillars on which a number of statutes were established. But these traditions were not written in a book. We have likewise shown that from that day the statutes were interpreted; the interpretations meant to make us understand the sense of the written word or phrase were not written, but the interpretations that add a condition, a limitation or an extension, and that do not lie in the sense of the word or phrase, were written; this is the character of the interpretations in Deuteronomy, and a few of them also in the other books. By this measure we can recognize the age of a given interpretation and know whether it is to be held as received or as new. We have also seen that the form of some statutes required some interpretation already at the time they were given, since they cannot be fulfilled unless we assume that their obscurities and generalities were made clear by the announcement or the knowledge of their details. Every seeker of the plain truth will admit that these judgments are just. But if in spite of all this we find many of the inquirers who deny everything, the blame does not lie with them but with the advocates of tradition and its lovers; for they kept no bound and went beyond measure. The words of the Talmud that ascribe the Mishnah and the Gemara and the sum of all the halakhot, the interpretations and the fine points to Moses at Sinai: all this they took literally. They did not consider whether this literal sense can stand against the contradictions that fall in it, and against the possibility that all the ancients said so for some particular purpose and reason. They were further strengthened in their view when they saw that some of the Geonim too understood the words as written, so that they said that even the discussions of the Amoraim were not of their own minds but were received (Epistle of R. Sherira Gaon), and that all the thirteen rules by which the Torah is expounded are received from Sinai (Rashi in the name of the Geonim, and Maimonides). And they did not consider the matter: that the Geonim too did not say so from a particular tradition, but on the strength of the proofs they brought from the words of the Talmud as written and in their plain sense. And if we look at the words of those who put questions before Rav Sherira Gaon on this point, we find that they too were entangled in doubts on this matter; necessarily, then, there was no public and known tradition. From this to extending tradition also to the halakhot of the later authorities, who derived consequences from the Talmud, is only one step. For since the whole body of the halakhot (and perhaps also of the aggadot) is tradition from Sinai, necessarily every consequence that comes out of it is in some measure tradition and counts as from Sinai. And it has already been said of R. Eliezer, author of the book *Roqeaḥ*, that he received the basis of the [laws of] penance that he composed from his teacher, and his teacher from his teacher, back to a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai (Responsa of Maharam, Prague edition, 113). But the enlightened will understand that such exaggeration did not help to strengthen the belief in the Oral Torah, but brought on it the opposition of every enlightened man, who will not be content with proofs of the truth of a thing when the proof itself still needs proof. Not so the proofs that we have laid down: they come from the content of the statutes themselves and from the time they were written in a book, and therefore they compel us to admit the existence of matters of tradition also from the side of inquiry and criticism. Yet how great is the number of the interpretations that survived from the first time? From the side of historical inquiry it is not in our power to decide, for we lack clear reports from the ancient times. But this we know: that in different times the statutes were interpreted in interpretations different from one another, as we shall see in the following chapters, and that they always fulfilled the statutes in practice according to their understanding of them; and that all of these rested on tradition is a thing that experience denies. But for the purpose that we set ourselves in this chapter it is enough that we have seen that the existence of traditions and oral matters in the early time has been confirmed for us, and that we have found the root and foundation for the spread of the belief in the Oral Torah.
The days of the Judges up to the days of Samuel the prophet

After the Israelites came to the rest and to the inheritance [Deuteronomy 12:9], their rest was nevertheless not complete and lasting; at times they had peace from their enemies round about, and at times they were oppressed. Their bad condition was always caused by their straying from the goal that the divine Lawgiver had set for them. All the days of the Judges they were like the degenerate shoots of a strange vine [Jeremiah 2:21] in the vineyard of the Lord of hosts. The bond of unity was slack among them; therefore the pillars of society tottered, and in all the affairs of this society there was no order. Time after time they turned from the way of their God, and when they turned away their shade too departed from them [Numbers 14:9]. The laws of their life and their customs were of mixed stock: half of them from the laws of the Torah and half from the laws of the nations round about them (1 Samuel 7:3). As this mixture grew, so in that measure the faithful traces of the Torah keep dwindling in all the accounts of the events in the time of the Judges. Only at rare times do we see a small spark of light from the traces of the Torah, which darkness takes away almost at once, and it is gone. And even in the moment when it shines and flashes it is not a bright light, but like a dim light glimmering out of the fog. Yet the weakness and the fewness of these traces will not keep us from finding in them too plain hints that teach us how some of the statutes of the Torah were understood at that time. True, not all that is told of their deeds is fit to show us the sense of the statutes; for many of these deeds were dross from a mixture of foreign laws that are not of Hebrew birth. And over many narratives a veil of poetic figure has been placed. But with a proper and measured examination we shall soon be able to tell the pure from the impure of foreign admixture. So too by reasoned inquiry we shall succeed in removing the veil, until we also succeed in knowing by which way of the spirit a given statute and law, written before us in the Torah, went to find its source in the custom of the people.⚠1

rows.en: Some narratives from the days of the Judges will be to us like a sealed book, unless we determine that the sense of some statutes that are obscure in the Torah was made clear among them, whether through a received and known interpretation or perhaps through a proper exegesis of the words of the statute. For all the days of Joshua and the elders the Israelites followed the Lord and served Him (Joshua 24:31); therefore every act of a religious kind that they did at that time was according to the Torah that Joshua received from Moses, and it is self-evident that the nature of the act will teach us how a given statute was understood which they had before their eyes in doing that act. The earliest and most compelling proof for the acceptance of the Oral Torah in its interpretation of the phrase "the morrow of the Sabbath," written with the counting of seven weeks from Passover to Pentecost [Leviticus 23:15], as referring to the morrow of the first day of Passover, comes to us from what is written in the book of Joshua (5:11): "And they ate of the produce of the land on the morrow of the Passover, unleavened bread and parched corn, in the selfsame day." These words, "unleavened bread and parched corn, in the selfsame day," refer without doubt to the statute in the Torah, "And ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn, nor fresh ears, until this selfsame day" [Leviticus 23:14]; and who can doubt that "the morrow of the Passover" here interprets "the morrow of the Sabbath" said there, and that its sense is as it was understood in the Oral Torah? It is all one to us whether "the morrow of the Passover" is understood as the fifteenth of Nisan (Ibn Ezra in Tosafot, Rosh Hashanah 13a) or as the sixteenth of Nisan (Ri in Tosafot there, and in Kiddushin 36b⚠1); in either case it is proved that this verse understood the phrase "the morrow of the Sabbath" as referring to the morrow of the Passover. So too we learn from the words of this book a new statute on the matter of the oath. When a man swears by the Lord, the God of Israel, he is bound to keep what has gone out of his lips, even if afterwards it becomes known that the reason that moved him to confirm a thing by oath was mistaken. And only for this reason did the princes (who had sworn to the Gibeonites by the Lord, the God of Israel, to make peace with them) see it as their duty to keep this oath, though it became known to them afterwards that the Gibeonites had come to them with guile. From this we see that the statute of the oath was understood among them thus: that in no case may a man transgress what has gone out of his lips in an oath, and also that in no case can the oath be annulled, and no man has the power to release it. And since there is no hint of all this in the Torah, necessarily this was the received interpretation among them. But this interpretation was abolished at a later time, and the sages of the Oral Torah turned away from it entirely. So too we are told that when Joshua made a covenant with the people and set them a statute and an ordinance in Shechem, he wrote the words in the book of the Torah of God, and took a great stone and set it up there under the oak that was by the sanctuary of the Lord (Joshua 24:26). Now when we read these words we necessarily recall the great warning with which the Torah warned to remove every asherah and to cut it down (Exodus 34:13). And in Deuteronomy this warning was extended also to planting near the altar of the Lord (Deuteronomy 15⚠2). Remembering this, shall we not ask how Joshua planted an oak in the sanctuary of the Lord, and acted against the plain sense of the verse that forbids all planting near the altar? And according to the sense of the words of the statute among the sages of the Oral Torah, the planting of any tree is forbidden both in the Chosen House, even on the Temple Mount, and at a high place (Sifre Shofetim, pisqa 145); necessarily, then, in the ancient days this statute was understood in another way: the asherah in its essence is the idol itself which the Canaanites worshipped, namely Ashtoreth. And since the form of this idol was a planted tree, on which perhaps the figure of the idol was itself carved, or an image was hung on it, it is proper to speak of planting and cutting down in its case. Now if they were warned against planting any tree near the altar, the intent was not to join the rite of the worship of the nations, who serve their gods, to the manner of the worship of the Lord in the sanctuary; but without intent of idolatry they saw no reason to be on guard. Therefore Joshua rightly did not hesitate to plant an oak in the sanctuary of the Lord, or, if it had been planted before, to leave it there without cutting it down. Two consequences follow for us from this. The one: the case of Joshua shows us in what way some statutes of the Torah were understood in the early time; and another: we see that the sense of these statutes changed in the course of time.

rows.en: In particular we must consider what traces there are among the narratives from the time of the Judges that let us recognize what their view was in those times regarding the sacrificial worship. True, it cannot be denied that at every step in the course of their history they turned from the statutes of the Torah and walked in the statutes of the nations, and these became a snare to them. Therefore it is hard for us to judge from their deeds about their views in the understanding of the statutes. Yet for all that there are some narratives of the events of that time on whose root views on the understanding of legal matters can be traced, especially regarding the worship of God in general and the sacrificial worship in particular. These views of theirs are hidden in subtle hints within the narratives. And if we wish to find these hidden things, we must first examine the nature of the sacrificial worship at its beginning, and what reason the Torah had to give it a place, since it is low in relation to God. On this the ancients already said: from days of old, sacrifices among men were signs of thanksgiving and of submission to God, and of the effort to win favour and atonement from Him. Israel in Egypt too were without doubt accustomed to some worship. Though we do not find that they sacrificed in Egypt, and on the contrary it is said, "Lo, shall we sacrifice the abomination of the Egyptians before their eyes, and will they not stone us?" [Exodus 8:22], at all events it is certain that they had a false worship like the worship of Egypt. And the Torah itself testified that they went astray after the satyrs and sacrificed their sacrifices to them [Leviticus 17:7]. Therefore we see that, according to the state of understanding in religious matters in these early times, the sacrificial worship was a religious worship of all the nations. There was no need to command it, for it was a thing understood of itself; but they were warned about the conditions and the forms. And since they were accustomed to sacrifice to the satyrs, they were commanded to bring their sacrifices to the door of the tent of meeting, so that they would no more sacrifice their sacrifices to the satyrs after whom they go astray, and would bring them to the Lord, whose dwelling was in the tent of meeting. So too in Deuteronomy they were commanded not to sacrifice except in the place which the Lord will choose. And all this so that the law of sacrifices would not be in the hand of each and every one, for otherwise they would easily turn from their God to go astray after other gods and serve them. Therefore, if we find that great and good men of the nation departed from the forms, this is a sign to us that they thought the form was only a fence against the breach and not an end in itself; and therefore, when the intent is acceptable, departing from the form does not prevent the acceptance of the sacrifice. And at special times we find that they sacrificed in every place, by the consent of the Torah or of their own accord. The Torah itself commanded to build an altar on Mount Ebal and to offer burnt offerings on it and to sacrifice peace offerings (Deuteronomy 26⚠1), and so Joshua did after crossing the Jordan (Joshua 8); Gideon built an altar and offered a sacrifice on it (Judges 10⚠2); the angel who came to Manoah said to him, "and if thou wilt offer a burnt offering, thou must offer it unto the Lord" (ibid. 13); Samuel offered a whole burnt offering at Mizpah (1 Samuel 7); so too the men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings when the ark of God returned from the field of the Philistines (ibid. 10⚠3); and at the renewal of Saul's kingship in Gilgal they sacrificed there sacrifices of peace offerings before the Lord (ibid. 11), and the tabernacle was not then at Gilgal. And after this too, when Saul smote the garrison of the Philistines, Saul offered the burnt offering at Gilgal (ibid. 13), and at Michmash too he built an altar (ibid. 14), and Samuel went to Bethlehem to sacrifice to the Lord (ibid. 15⚠4). All these are deeds actually done, and they testify that in all the early times they were not strict about sacrificing in every place; though there is no clear proof in the verses according to their plain sense that it was permitted to sacrifice at a high place at any of the times from when they crossed the Jordan and settled in the land. True, the sages of the Talmud expounded the verses by the ways of their midrash in a manner far from the plain sense. And even with their midrash they found no just ground to show a definite permission explicit in Scripture, but they judged from the later to the earlier. That is: from what is told in Scripture, that they were accustomed to sacrifice at a high place and it was not counted to them as sin, from this they judged that they necessarily knew it was permitted by the Torah. And in the Talmud they said that at one time the high places were forbidden and at another time permitted (Zevaḥim 112b; Sifre Re'eh, pisqa 66); and this wording shows that they were forbidden and permitted by the word of a prophet or of someone else. Since we saw them sacrificing at a high place, they necessarily judged that it had been permitted to them. And if we ask what reason they saw to permit sacrifice at a high place against the Torah, they found no other reason than to say that it was a temporary ruling (Zevaḥim, ibid.). This excuse was always in their mouth when they found in Scripture that the prophets or other men of rank acted with sacrifices not according to the Torah, whether in sacrificing at a high place or in departing in some other way from the statutes regarding the form of the sacrifice and its offering (Avodah Zarah 24b). Yet if we consider the matter, this excuse does not suffice in every place to quiet the doubts. When Gideon offered a burnt offering to the Lord, he offered it with the wood of the asherah (Judges 6), and he offered the second bullock that belonged to his father, which (according to the opinion of the Talmud) his father had set apart to offer to idolatry (Temurah 28b); and all this is against the statute of the Torah as it was understood by the sages of the Oral Torah; for according to that understanding the wood of an asherah may not come on the altar, nor may a sacrifice to the Lord be brought from what was set apart for idolatry. True, the Talmud found an explanation, saying that this was an exception, because Gideon did all this by the word of the Lord. But though this may suffice as an excuse for Gideon, we still do not know why the Lord commanded him to do in this way a deed against the law. And even if we assume there was a need of the hour to sacrifice, we see no need and necessity on that account to offer specifically the second bullock that was set apart for idolatry (as they understood it in the Talmud); could he not have offered the first bullock? And likewise, why did He command him to sacrifice with the wood of the asherah: did he have no other wood? It can only be that in the ancient days even the great and the good were not so strict about the forms, but thought that the form was only a fence against the breach and not an end in itself, and therefore, when the intent is acceptable, departing from the form does not prevent the acceptance of the sacrifice. And though it cannot be denied that there was an existing and known statute that one may not sacrifice in every place, nevertheless it also cannot be denied that they were not strict about this in a worship done occasionally, for the hour, and with the intent of the sake of the Lord. Only for the fixing of the sacrificial worship was the Torah strict, that it be fixed in one place only, because fixing it in different places is dangerous to the unity of the nation, and it would also easily become to them a snare of idolatry. As we see explicitly in the story of the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben and the half-tribe of Manasseh: all the alarm that their brethren across the Jordan, in the land of Canaan, raised against them when they built an altar was only because they thought that they had built an altar for burnt offering and for sacrifice, and they saw in this rebellion and trespass against the Lord (Joshua 22). But as regards the acceptance of the sacrifice, all depends on the intent and the thought of the worshipper; and therefore occasionally and for the hour one may sacrifice in every place. And perhaps this is how the statute of the Torah was understood which commands that they may make an altar of earth to offer on it burnt offering or sacrifice, and in every place where His name is remembered He will come to them and bless them (Exodus 21⚠5). For from the tenor of these words it appears that all places are fit for sacrificing there, provided only that the sacrifice be for the sake of the Lord. And what is said in other places, to beware of sacrificing in another place than the place which the Lord will choose, is surely to be explained in the way we have said.{v1_02_13:1} And from the time the kingdom was divided there is no doubt that they offered sacrifices in the land of the kingdom of Israel on altars that they built for the sake of the Lord, and all this was with the consent of the prophets; for otherwise how is it possible that Elijah the prophet should complain that the altars dedicated to the Lord were torn down, if these altars stood against the Torah and in prohibition (1 Kings 19:10, 14)?

rows.en: Another part of the worship of the Lord was the vow. And we find a wonderful example of a vow in an early time, and of the manner of its fulfilment, in the vow of Jephthah. This judge, on going out to war against the Ammonites, vowed a vow: "If the Lord deliver the children of Ammon into my hand, then whatsoever cometh forth of the doors of my house to meet me shall surely be the Lord's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering" (Judges 11). And as he prospered in his way and returned, behold, his only daughter came to meet him. And when he saw this evil occurrence he rent his clothes, for he said, "I have opened my mouth unto the Lord, and I cannot go back"; and at the end of two months he did with her according to his vow which he had vowed. Here we see that in these early times it was the custom to offer a human soul as a burnt offering to the Lord, the God of Israel; for if this had been against the law, the words put in Jephthah's mouth would be words without sense. How could he say, "I have opened my mouth unto the Lord, and I cannot go back," if the fulfilment of his vow was counted an abomination in the eyes of the Lord and a sin of bloodshed? And it is no wonder that such a false and cruel belief was not cut off at once from among the nation, for since they became a people they grew up and lived among the nations who held this belief. True, the divine statutes strove with all their might to cut it off, in warning against the worship of Molech; and perhaps the sanctity of the human firstborn too was meant to stand in place of the sacrifice of their sons, which all the nations of the East practised.{v1_02_14:1} But in spite of all this the false belief still kept root and branch among Israel. The fixed worship of human sacrifice was decreed against and cut off, but it still continued occasionally among individuals, and it was not counted among them as opposed to the religion of the Torah of Moses to offer a human sacrifice in thanksgiving for a great deliverance by which they were saved, or to quiet the anger of the Lord and to appease Him; for they found no definite statute against human sacrifice, and though it is said, "of the herd and of the flock shall ye bring your offering" [Leviticus 1:2], they erred in thinking that this does not exclude human sacrifice in great and special events. Only by this can we understand that Jephthah fulfilled his vow against his will, and that there was no man who set his mind to say that there was no duty to fulfil his vow, and that on the contrary it was his duty not to fulfil it, for human sacrifice is an abomination in the eyes of God, and the Lord did not accept it. And perhaps this corrupt view came to them from a terrible error by which they erred in the sense of the pure words of the Torah, and they twisted and corrupted its pleasant words: either the story of Abraham's binding of Isaac confused their mind, or perhaps they likewise understood, in this corrupt sense, the words of the Torah in the affair of Baal Peor, where the Lord commanded Moses, at the time when the people sinned and went astray with the daughters of Moab and joined themselves to Baal Peor, to take all the heads of the people and hang them up unto the Lord before the sun, that the fierce anger of the Lord may turn away from Israel (Numbers 25:4). And seeing that by the command of the Lord they were hanged up to the Lord, not for their own sin (for they had not sinned) but only to turn away the fierce anger of the Lord, they judged from this that human sacrifice for atonement was not abhorred in the eyes of the Lord. But the prophets, they taught the view that the Lord does not delight in many sacrifices, and does not desire that a man give his firstborn for his transgression, the fruit of his body for the sin of his soul, to make atonement (Micah 6:7). And with a zeal like fire Jeremiah was zealous against those who thought that God's will lay in human sacrifices, and he said that the Lord did not command so, and it did not come into His heart.{v1_02_14:2} From all this we see that in different times the words of the Torah too were understood in different ways. And beyond what we have seen so far from the case of Jephthah, we see further that in those days it was not possible to annul a vow in any way, even if the one who vowed regretted it; for otherwise, did not Jephthah regret his vow, and could they not have annulled it? Why then did they not annul it or release it (Genesis Rabbah 60)? Therefore it is a clear thing that the power to annul a vow that a man vows, by means of release, which has no foundation except in the oral tradition, was not yet known in this early time; and the bearers of the Torah of that time too did not know it, did not receive it and did not hand it down (see Ḥagigah 10a and Rashi's commentary), as we have already seen in the oath of the princes to the Gibeonites.

In all these contradictions it is said in the wording "one verse says," etc. Sifra, Vayikra, chapter 3, mishnah 1⚠1; Beḥukkotai, chapter 1; and in Sifre Naso, pisqa 42, and see pisqa 124⚠2, and in several places. So too in countless places in the Talmud, among them Sotah (26b), Bava Metzia (33a), Ḥullin (24a, 81a, 90a), Arakhin (29a), Menaḥot (62a), (66a); and in all these places you will see that they decided of their own minds. And in the manuscript book called *Mar Qashisha*, by the rabbi who wrote *Ḥavvot Ya'ir*, which is from the library of the Beit ha-Midrash under the direction of Rabbi Aaron Jellinek in the city of Vienna, the author, in the entry "Two verses," criticizes the rabbi who wrote *Qorban Aharon*, and he laboured and took pains to copy most of the places in the Talmud where two contradictory verses are brought and the sages decided between them of their own minds; and he agrees with the view of the Rabad.
